entries.answer:
The uploaded technical description is an 80,841-character HTML/SVG capture of a graphical interface rather than a concise requirements document. It depicts a responsive asset-selection and file-management interface, including an asset picker, searchable grid, filtering controls, selectable file cards, and destructive-delete confirmation dialogs.[1]

## Comprehensive Build Prompt

```text
Construct a complete, production-ready, full-stack web application that provides an image and media asset-management interface with a responsive asset-selection modal, searchable and filterable asset grid, per-file metadata, selectable assets, and safe deletion workflows.

Deliver every source file required to build, run, test, and deploy the system. Include complete, unabridged production code; package manifests; lockfiles where applicable; configuration files; database schema and migrations; API routes; frontend components; stylesheets; test suites; environment-variable templates; containerization files; documentation; and automated validation scripts. Do not omit implementation details, substitute partial code, use mock components, or rely on placeholder functionality.

Do not reproduce any product name, brand identity, proprietary logo, proprietary source code, proprietary asset, original UI text that identifies a third-party service, or any protected visual identity from the supplied technical description. Implement the described behavior and interaction model independently with original structure, styling, copy, icons, and naming.

Build the application in the following order.

1. Establish the repository structure.

Create a monorepo or clearly separated frontend and backend packages. Use TypeScript throughout. Include a root README that documents prerequisites, installation, environment setup, database initialization, local development, testing, production build, containerized deployment, and operational behavior.

Use a modern frontend framework with server-rendering support where beneficial. Use a typed backend API. Use a relational database for durable persistence. Use object storage compatible with local development and cloud deployment for uploaded original media and derived outputs. Use a migration-based ORM or database toolkit. Include Docker Compose for local orchestration of the application, database, object storage emulator or compatible storage service, and any required worker process.

2. Define the domain model.

Implement persistent entities for:

- User: authenticated account identity, profile data, timestamps, and authorization fields.
- Workspace: isolated ownership boundary for assets and user membership.
- WorkspaceMember: user-to-workspace role assignment.
- Asset: unique identifier, workspace identifier, original filename, normalized display filename, media type, MIME type, byte size, checksum, storage key, width, height, duration when applicable, creation timestamp, update timestamp, deletion status, source/original flag, parent asset identifier for derivatives, processing status, and searchable text fields.
- AssetVersion or DerivedAsset: relationship to an original asset, transformation metadata, output storage key, status, dimensions, MIME type, and timestamps.
- DeletionJob or AuditLog: actor identity, target asset identity, operation type, result status, timestamps, and failure details when an asset or derived version is removed.
- UploadSession or UploadJob: upload state, expected checksum, multipart metadata if applicable, retry state, and finalization state.
- AssetSelectionSession where needed to persist or transmit selected asset identifiers.

Enforce referential integrity. Deleting an original asset must atomically delete or soft-delete all derived assets that depend on it. The system must not leave orphaned database rows or orphaned stored files. Use transactions for database mutations and an idempotent cleanup strategy for storage deletion.

3. Build authentication and authorization.

Implement secure authentication and session management. Require an authenticated user for all asset actions. Enforce workspace membership for every query and mutation. Never expose asset metadata, thumbnails, originals, or derived outputs across workspace boundaries.

Implement role checks for destructive actions. Return structured API errors for unauthorized access, invalid input, unavailable assets, conflicts, and storage-processing failures. Log server-side errors without exposing internal stack traces to the browser.

4. Implement media upload and processing.

Provide a complete upload pipeline for supported image types, including JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF where supported, and other explicitly configured formats. Validate MIME type by inspecting file signatures rather than trusting only client-provided metadata. Enforce configurable upload-size and image-dimension limits. Generate a cryptographic checksum to detect duplicates or corrupted transfers.

Store the original upload as the source asset. Generate optimized thumbnails and previews asynchronously or through a reliable background process. Persist processing state so the interface can display a loading state while previews are unavailable. If thumbnail generation fails, retain the original asset, mark processing as failed, record the error, and make retry behavior available through a secured endpoint.

Create signed or access-controlled URLs for original files, thumbnails, and derived files. Do not expose permanent public object-storage URLs unless explicitly configured for public workspaces.

5. Implement asset-listing APIs.

Create paginated APIs that return assets for the active workspace. Support:

- Text search across original filename, display filename, user-provided labels, and selected metadata.
- Asset scope filter with at least:
  - all assets, including originals and derived outputs;
  - original assets only, excluding derived outputs.
- Sort options with at least newest first and oldest first.
- Stable cursor pagination suitable for large libraries.
- Filtering by processing state and media type if the frontend exposes these controls.
- Accurate total or approximate-count strategy documented in the API contract.
- Asset response fields sufficient to render cards without issuing one request per asset.

Expose a dedicated endpoint to obtain a single asset and its derived versions. Return a normalized representation with secure preview URLs, status data, dimensions, file size, timestamps, and relationship information.

6. Implement deletion APIs and background cleanup.

Create an authenticated deletion endpoint for one asset at a time. The deletion request must identify the asset by its immutable ID, verify workspace ownership and user authorization, determine whether the target is an original or derived asset, and calculate all dependent records and storage objects that must be removed.

If an original asset is deleted, delete all derived versions associated with that original. If a derived asset is deleted independently, remove only that derivative unless the product rules require otherwise. Record every deletion request and outcome in the audit log.

Use a two-stage deletion flow:
- Mark database records as pending deletion inside a transaction.
- Delete storage objects through a reliable worker or transactional outbox process.
- Finalize deletion after storage cleanup succeeds.
- Retry failed cleanup safely and visibly to operators.
- Ensure repeat requests are idempotent and return a meaningful response rather than producing inconsistent state.

7. Build the responsive asset-selection interface.

Create a modal-based asset picker that can be opened from any consumer workflow in the application. The modal must be fully keyboard accessible and use an accessible dialog implementation.

The modal must include:

- A header containing a descriptive title such as “Choose media to attach.”
- A close button with a clear accessible label.
- A search field with an inline search icon and a meaningful placeholder.
- A grouped scope toggle with an “All” option and an “Originals” option. “All” is selected by default.
- A sort button that opens an accessible menu for sort direction and any supported sort modes.
- A responsive asset grid inside a scrollable content area.
- An empty state for no search results.
- A loading state while the first page or subsequent pages are being fetched.
- An error state with a retry action when listing fails.
- Infinite scrolling or an explicit “Load more” control that works with keyboard and screen readers.
- A footer containing selection count, cancel behavior, and a primary action that returns the selected asset IDs to the calling workflow.

Use a grid whose column count adapts to viewport width. On narrow mobile layouts, render one card per row or a compact single-column layout. On larger screens, progressively increase columns according to available width while maintaining a usable minimum card width. Avoid horizontal page overflow.

8. Implement asset cards.

Each asset card must include:

- A selectable checkbox or checkbox-equivalent control with a visible selected state and a programmatic selected state.
- A thumbnail area with a stable aspect ratio.
- A background placeholder while the thumbnail loads.
- A loading indicator while thumbnail generation or retrieval is pending.
- A broken-preview fallback when preview retrieval fails.
- A visible filename, truncated safely without losing the full name from accessible text or a tooltip.
- A concise source classification such as “Original” or “Derived.”
- Optional metadata such as dimensions, file size, and date when the layout has enough space.
- A contextual actions control where allowed, including deletion.
- Focus indicators, keyboard selection behavior, and semantic labels.

Support single-select and multi-select modes through a configuration prop or component API. In multi-select mode, do not close the modal when a card is selected. Preserve selection while fetching additional pages, changing sort order, and filtering, unless an item becomes unavailable.

9. Implement deletion confirmation.

When a user invokes deletion from an asset card or details view, open a confirmation dialog. The dialog must:

- Name the exact target asset using its display filename.
- Explain that dependent edited or derived versions will also be removed when the target is an original.
- Provide a non-destructive cancel action.
- Provide a clearly visually distinct destructive confirmation action.
- Prevent accidental execution through Escape, backdrop click behavior, or focus loss from triggering deletion.
- Disable duplicate submission while deletion is in progress.
- Display a success notification after completion.
- Display an actionable failure notification if deletion fails.
- Remove the deleted asset from visible lists immediately after confirmed success, or mark it as pending removal if cleanup is asynchronous.
- Update selection state so deleted items are not returned as selected assets.

Use original dialog copy and original styling. Do not duplicate exact interface wording from any referenced system.

10. Implement frontend state management.

Use a typed query and mutation layer with cache invalidation or optimistic updates. Keep asset list state synchronized across the grid, search field, filters, sort menu, details view, and deletion flow. Debounce search input without delaying immediate clearing. Cancel obsolete requests when filters or queries change. Protect against out-of-order API responses overwriting newer search results.

Store transient modal state locally unless it needs to survive navigation. Store server-backed asset state in a normalized cache or a clearly documented query system. Ensure selection handling is deterministic and resilient to pagination.

11. Implement accessibility.

Conform to WCAG 2.2 AA practices across the interface. Provide:

- Correct modal focus trapping and focus restoration.
- Semantic buttons, checkboxes, menus, dialog labels, and descriptions.
- Keyboard navigation for search, scope toggles, sort menu, grid cards, checkboxes, actions menus, and dialogs.
- Visible focus styles.
- Screen-reader announcements for loading, result counts, selection changes, deletion outcomes, and validation errors.
- Sufficient color contrast.
- No information conveyed by color alone.
- Support for reduced motion preferences.
- Touch targets appropriate for mobile use.

12. Implement visual design independently.

Create an original visual system suitable for a modern content-management application. Use a restrained neutral background, clear typography, layered surfaces, compact controls, responsive spacing, readable file labels, subtle borders, and a distinct destructive-action treatment. Use independently created SVG icons or an open icon library under a compatible license. Do not copy visual assets, class names, markup structure, proprietary terminology, or exact styling from the supplied material.

13. Implement robust API validation and observability.

Validate every API request with explicit schemas. Rate-limit uploads and destructive operations. Add structured logs for upload initiation, upload completion, thumbnail generation, listing queries, selection submissions where applicable, deletion attempts, cleanup retries, and failures. Add health and readiness endpoints. Ensure secrets are loaded only from environment variables and are never committed.

Provide audit-friendly request IDs and error IDs in API responses. Add metrics hooks or a documented instrumentation interface for asset count, processing duration, upload failures, thumbnail failures, deletion success rate, and cleanup retry rate.

14. Implement testing.

Write complete automated tests, including:

- Unit tests for file validation, checksum handling, scope filtering, sorting, pagination cursor handling, authorization, deletion dependency resolution, and cleanup idempotency.
- Integration tests for upload, asset listing, search, originals-only filtering, thumbnail processing status, asset selection, deletion confirmation request handling, original-with-derivatives deletion, derived-only deletion, and authorization isolation.
- End-to-end browser tests for opening the picker, searching, changing scope, sorting, selecting items, submitting selection, invoking deletion, canceling deletion, confirming deletion, responsive layout behavior, keyboard navigation, focus management, and error recovery.
- Accessibility tests for dialogs, forms, menus, cards, and notifications.
- Tests that confirm no orphaned derived assets or storage-object references remain after source deletion.

15. Deliver complete documentation.

Document the architecture, repository layout, data model, API endpoints, authentication model, authorization rules, storage configuration, asynchronous processing mechanism, deletion guarantees, testing commands, deployment instructions, operational troubleshooting, and configuration reference.

Include a complete environment template containing all required variables with descriptive comments. Include instructions for local object storage, database migration execution, creating the initial user or workspace, and running the worker process.

16. Define acceptance criteria.

The completed application must allow an authorized user to upload original image assets, see processing states, browse assets in a responsive grid, search by filename, toggle between all assets and originals only, change sort order, select one or more items, return selected asset identifiers to a caller, and delete an asset only after explicit confirmation.

Deleting an original asset must also remove all linked derived versions. The UI must clearly communicate this consequence before confirmation. The application must function correctly on mobile and desktop layouts, remain usable by keyboard and screen-reader users, enforce workspace isolation, survive network failures gracefully, and include full code and automated tests for all described behavior.
```

## Notes on the extracted specification

The supplied capture explicitly shows the core interaction elements reflected in the prompt: an “All” versus originals-only scope toggle, filename search, a sort control, selectable file tiles, loading thumbnail placeholders, source-image labeling, and deletion dialogs warning that edited versions will also be deleted.[1]

The prompt intentionally treats the material as behavioral and structural input only: it requires an original implementation rather than reproducing source markup, internal test IDs, CSS class names, specific SVG paths, visual branding, or protected interface copy.
